newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: OPPOSITION, DEMOCRATS DEMAND COLSTON'S HEAD
The Opposition and the Democrats are demanding the resignation from Parliament of Independent Senator, Mal Colston, after a decision to refer fraud allegations against him to the Federal Police.
Prime Minister, John Howard, made the decision to refer the case to the A-F-P after new information came to light last night.
Mr Howard acted after seeing a letter sent to Senate President Margaret Reid by the solicitors of Christine Smith, Senator Colston's former office manager.
In the letter, Mrs Smith retracts an earlier statement in which she took responsibility for wrongly claimed travel allowances by Senator Colston.
Mr Howard says the letter fundamentally changes the situation, and has called on Senator Colston to stand down as Deputy President of the Senate.
But Democrats leader, Cheryl Kernot, says the most honourable thing Senator Colston can do at the end of what she calls a "very grubby affair", is to resign from the Senate.
FINANCIAL SECTOR REVIEW TO BE RELEASED TODAY
The future of Australia's financial system will become a little clearer today with the publication of the Wallis inquiry, and the Government's response to it.
The inquiry, headed by Stan Wallis, takes a fresh look at current regulatory structures which date back to the early 1980s, when the Campbell inquiry ushered in de-regulation and flexibility.
When launching the Wallis inquiry last May, Federal Treasurer Peter Costello said it was needed because current arrangements have reached their use-by date.
It's expected the inquiry will allow mergers among the biggest banks and life insurers.
Consumer groups say this would lead to bank branch closures and job losses.
It will also cover foreign ownership, regulation of the sector and opening the payments system to non-banks.
CARR URGED TO COME CLEAN ON "CASINO AFFAIR"

The New South Wales Government has used its numbers in parliament to defeat an Opposition motion demanding the Premier reveal the source of material he used to damage Showboat's bid for the Sydney casino.
A-B-C Television's Four Corners program has raised questions about how Bob Carr came by information linking a member of the Showboat consortium with the Mafia.
Mr Carr refused to divulge his source and claims his actions were vindicated by an inquiry.
Opposition leader, Peter Collins, has appealed to the Premier to come clean about what he's called the Casino Affair.
CHAOS EXPECTED ON MELBOURNE'S TRAINS
Melbourne's public transport system will be in chaos this morning as dozens of trains are left out of action because of a maintenance workers strike.
The 24-hour-strike is due to finish at eight o'clock, but it will take some hours for normal services to resume.
The Public Transport Corporation says delays of up to 15 minutes are likely throughout the network.
It's urging people to arrive at stations early and be patient.
The strike is part of an on-going dispute about wages, superannuation and work conditions.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
